Forbes had some issues with bernie sanders' economic policies. Are these criticisms valid?

Very. As the author points out, some of Sanders ideas are perfectly sensible (like cutting military spending), but many of his enhanced taxation ideas are not very well thought out. The "Robin Hood" taxation system of taking from the rich to give to the poor sounds nice in theory, but when actually put into practice and studied, it typically hurts more than it helps.

One way in which this is especially true is Sanders' ideas for continuing to fund Social Security through more taxes rather than by reforming the program itself: thanks to the fact that life expectancies continue to increase, the cost of SS and Medicare will simply continue to increase unless the retirement age is increased as well. Finding ways to pay for these programs is an endless and fruitless struggle if we don't control their costs.

Overall, it's a very fair article, pointing out both the strengths and weaknesses of Sanders' various ideas. A good read for his supporters.

Can you explain why Sanders' 0.03% tax on speculations is a bad idea? I thought the author did a really shitty job explaining that, aside from wrapping it up with the blanket statement of "it's bad for the economy, and it would shrink the economy."

I'm pretty sure the average American isn't speculating on the stock market, so wouldn't this tax only affect some of the richest, most economically savvy Americans?

Indeed, one of Sanders' main points is that we should not be worrying so much about "the economy" if it serves to enrich only the wealthiest Americans.

As the article points out, studies indicate that a tax of that type reduces economic growth by discouraging investment: it might seem like a tiny tax would only make a tiny difference, but as Sanders himself points out there are so many investments that it makes a pretty sizable difference in the long run.

As for his suggestion that we simply shouldn't care about economic growth, he couldn't be more wrong on that note. The entire reason that your quality of life is better than that of a person in the Congo is because of growth: the computer on which you're reading this wasn't redistributed from any wealthy person nor stolen from poor people who originally owned it. 99% of people who have ever been raised out of poverty in the entire history of human civilization have achieved wealth through growth.

In this way, growth is extremely important in the long run, for a future we can't even foresee now. If we had applied Sanders' reasoning consistently for the last 1,000 years, we'd all be living pretty nice, equal lives with little wealth inequality - by the standards of the middle ages. We wouldn't even know what we'd be missing, just like now neither of us can foresee exactly what future growth will bring us. The problem with that approach is that it gives a quick payout at the expense of a much greater long-term gain, and that's why growth matters.

To counter your point on economic growth--there is no more upward mobility in America anymore. When 99% of all economic growth goes to the top 1/10 of the 1%, these sorts of taxes really have no effect on the average American. Trickle down economics is a proven farce.

Right now the average American is bruised and beaten by an economic system that is indifferent to his suffering. Personally, I do not think that a 0.03% tax would discourage investment, because the people who it affects have the spare cash to eat the tax.

And please, the middle ages? Sanders' policies will not stagnate the economy, they will enrich the consumer base, allowing for greater growth for everyone in the long run, even if it means an initial dip in "economic prosperity" for those at the very top of the economic system.

Ensuring that growth benefits everyone is fine - a good thing, even. But trying to do so is counter-productive when it inhibits growth from occurring in the first place. It would be nice if fixing the problem were as simple as redistribution, but the evidence indicates that it isn't: like it or not, these policies have a demonstrable impact on long-term growth, and do result in stagnant economies. Just look at Sweden, a model Sanders himself says we should follow, which has had no net growth in the last 20 years.

Growing in a way that benefits everyone is a good idea, but there are ways to achieve that that don't prevent growth from happening, which is unfortunately what many of Sanders' ideas would cause.

Looking at the graph you provided, it's clear that Sweden has had economic growth in the past 20 years. Yes, there are a few years where percent growth dips below 0 (notably during the 2008 recession, caused by the disastrous policies of Sanders' opposition), but overall it looks as though Sweden has maintained a modest rate of growth over the past 20 years. You are right to say that their rate of growth has not increased substantially, but growth is absolutely present.

Though you seem to have some other ideas about how to create economic growth for everyone. Care to share an alternative to Sanders' plan?

By the way, thanks for having a genuine, intelligent, level-headed discussion about this!

It has a very small amount, and upon further examination growth there has only slowed as more and more growth-stifling measures have been enacted. At this rate it actually will grind to a complete halt within the next decade or so. That might seem nice for now as the middle class has a lot of benefits, but what about 50 years from now when the country has fallen behind its neighbors?

As for alternatives, I support a small government bereft of the tools it currently uses to prop up entrenched corporate interests. Sanders is right that we have a problem with these interests, but the real cause of them is that government has increasingly propped them up. He's right that we should stop subsidizing them, but his plan for replacing the subsidies with penalties is shortsighted.

The thing about government is that it will always be unfairly influenced by major interests: money will always find a way into the system, as countless "people's" revolutions have learned the hard way in the past. You can't get money out of politics, but you can neuter politics such that it no longer has the power to prop up these groups. Move the subsidies around, and they'll find their way back to those with influence; remove the subsidies altogether, and you actually solve the problem.
